Abel Ferro, the tuner, reached the Pellam Street hall on a snowy Thursday, two days before Lise Marrow's recital. Lise, the town's best young pianist, said the old upright had been sounding wrong all winter, with a buzz somewhere in the bass. Nell Ostrand, the hall's manager, had sent for him, and Edith Garvey, the hall's benefactor, had offered the committee the gift of a new piano if the old one proved worn out.

Nell had found the crack in March, dusting under the lid, and she told Owen Dorran, the caretaker, then Lise, then Mrs. Garvey, all in one breathless afternoon. Abel saw it for the first time now: a hairline split in the board that had opened since the last entry in the notebook of his old teacher, Tobias Rusk. For thirty years Rusk had tuned this piano a shade below standard pitch, and Abel had kept to that pitch at each October tuning since, at the committee's expense. Lise had learned on it.

The piano stood where it always had, at the far end from the stove. Abel struck the low C, and the buzz came at once. One bass string had snapped near its pin, and the loose end lay rattling against its neighbours. He fitted a new string from his case and tuned it to match the rest, at Rusk's pitch.

'Will it be ready for Saturday?' Nell asked. Abel, who had shared a desk with her at school forty years before, held up the broken string between two fingers. 'In ten minutes. Here is the monster that sent you running to Mrs. Garvey. Shall we have it framed for the committee room?' He coiled it and dropped it into her palm with a little bow.

On Saturday Lise went through her whole programme without a sour note, and the new string sat among the old ones as if it had always been there. Mrs. Garvey kept her money for a new piano another year, for the committee to accept when the old one truly wore out. Abel, listening from the back row, heard the low C ring true on the final chord.

passage:
For forty-six summers a carousel turned on Larkmoor common, its twenty-four horses carved in 1912 by Josiah Fenn. When it closed in 1958, the council sold it off piece by piece, and the horses went to families across the valley who bought them for a few shillings each.

Nora Quill had ridden those horses as a girl. In 1991, newly retired from the post office, she found the auction ledger among some council papers, and began drafting a long letter to the council on why the carousel should stand on the common. The ledger gave only lot numbers, but a faded photograph taken in 1923 showed each horse's name painted on its saddle, and with it she matched every lot to a horse and found the families easily. The first horse she brought home had been displayed in a hotel lobby in Brannock. After it came horses from a saddler's shop, a school hall, a chapel basement and an ivied garden, until every horse but one was back.

The original colours were the hard part. Every family had repainted its horse several times, and beneath the layers the oldest paint had gone to powder. For three years Nora and a retired chemist took the coats off a square inch at a time. The rest went quickly. A raffle raised four thousand pounds across the town, and the money paid for the restoration; the band organ, its painted front intact, needed only new bellows; and the council agreed in one evening that the carousel should stand on the common, so the letter went unsent.

That left the grey, which Hal Brigg's father had bought at the auction. Sure of her welcome, Nora told the Courier the grey would be home by Easter before writing to Hal, and he read it there first. When she did ask, his answer was two lines: she might have asked a man before announcing his property in the paper, and she could come and discuss it once she had learned some manners.

The grey came home in June, after Nora drove out to the Brigg farm to apologise. The carousel turned again on the common that July, every horse in place.

passage:
For sixteen summers Dr. Hana Vell has counted the sand beetles of Orsk Spit, pale hunters the size of a thumbnail. They spend the day in burrows in the upper dune and cross the dune foot each night to catch sand fleas along the tide line. Every July Vell sets forty pitfall traps along the dune crest. Last July, her student Joel Arkin's first on the spit, the count fell from its usual eight hundred to two hundred and sixty.

Much had changed on the spit that year. Over the winter the park had put up a sand fence along the south end of the dune foot, beside the car park. A March storm cut into the dune's seaward face, though the crest and the traps came through it. In May a boardwalk opened, with lamps that switch off at ten, hours before the beetles stir; the park had wanted them on all night, but the power bill ran to nine thousand dollars a year. Visitors wore paths across the north hollow, a kilometre past the last trap.

Arkin spent his first week digging test pits where the storm had cut the dune, and found the burrows whole and full. Vell went to her notebooks. The spit's one earlier drop, in 2013, had looked just like this one: a fall by two thirds in a single July, then a slow climb back over two summers while the park left the dune as it was. It had recovered by itself.

Arkin brought Vell a letter asking the park to take down the fence and switch off the lamps, the third such letter he had drafted that week, and asked her to sign it. Vell handed it back unsigned, with the 2013 pages clipped to the front, and told him to read them before he wrote a fourth.

Vell left the traps and the spit exactly as they were. This July, with the fence, the lamps and the visitors all still there, the count climbed back to seven hundred and forty.
